tone_statements.citation: Connell, Bruce. 2000. The integrity of Mambiloid. In H. Ekkehard Wolff & Orin Gensler (eds.), Proceedings of the 2nd World Congress of African Linguistics, Leipzig 1997, 197-213. Cologne: Rüdiger Köppe.
tone_statements.quote: Mambiloid languages appear all to have either three or four tones. The four tone systems are plausibly a development of an earlier three tone system, while the three tone systems constitute an innovation relative to two tone systems found in related languages outside Mambiloid (Connell 1997a).
tone_statements.locator: HTML version, section 3.3 'Phonological characteristics' (printed pagination 197-213 not reproduced in the HTML)
tone_statements.summary: Group-level: every Mambiloid language has three or four (level) tones; three-tone systems seen as a split from an earlier two-tone system conditioned by lost class-prefix tones; nothing on contours, TBU or stress for Ndoola specifically.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote verified verbatim at the stated locator in the extracted text file we hold. (2) The deciding source is a preliminary wordlist-based sketch, but it is by a Mambiloid phonologist (Connell), the wordlist is consistently tone-marked with three levels, and it is the only phonological description of Ndoola that exists: Glottolog has no grammar/phonology/sketch entry and a web search found nothing beyond pages that cite this same ms. (3) Nothing open could be downloaded that bears on stress; works still to obtain are low-priority comparative/unpublished materials. (4) Coding 'tonal' (tonal-OR-pitch accent, domain not stated by the source) follows from an explicit three-level tone statement with silence on stress; no better source is likely to change it, so status adequate (not well-sourced only because the source is a skeleton preliminary ms rather than a full description), action none. Minor non-coding fix available:

tone.says: Sec. 3.3 'Phonological characteristics' states that Mambiloid languages all appear to have either three or four tones, four-tone systems developing from an earlier three-tone system and three tones being an innovation relative to two-tone relatives outside Mambiloid (Connell 1997a: tonal split conditioned by the tone of a former class prefix); no word-stress statement; consistent with the three level tones (H, M, L) our catalog records for Ndoola from Connell & Blench.
